/-!
# Green's Open Problem 47

*References:*
- [Gr24] [Ben Green's 100 Open Problems](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.47)
- [GH14] Green, Ben, and Adam J. Harper. "Inverse questions for the large sieve."
  Geometric and Functional Analysis 24.4 (2014): 1167-1203.
- [HV09] Helfgott, Harald Andrés, and Akshay Venkatesh. "How small must ill-distributed sets be."
  Analytic number theory 2 (2009): 224-234.
- [Wa12] Walsh, Miguel N. "The inverse sieve problem in high dimensions." (2012): 2001-2022.
- [Wa14] Walsh, Miguel N. "The algebraicity of ill-distributed sets."
  Geometric and Functional Analysis 24.3 (2014): 959-967.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Green47

/--
Suppose that a large sieve process leaves a set of quadratic size. Is that set quadratic?

The following very particular instance is probably the simplest [Gr24]:
Suppose that $A \subset \mathbb{N}$ is a set with the property that
$|A \pmod p| \leqslant \frac{1}{2}(p + 1)$ for all sufficiently large $p$.
Is it true that either $|A \cap [X]| \ll X^{1/2} / \log^{100} X$, or $A$ is contained in the
image of $\mathbb{Z}$ under a quadratic map $\phi : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem green_47 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ A : Set ℕ,
      (∀ᶠ p in atTop, Nat.Prime p → Set.ncard (Set.image (fun a : ℕ => (a : ZMod p)) A) ≤ (p + 1) / 2) →
      ((fun X : ℕ => ((A ∩ Set.Iic X).ncard : ℝ)) ≪ (fun X : ℕ => Real.sqrt (X : ℝ) / (Real.log (X : ℝ)) ^ 100))
      ∨ (∃ P : Polynomial ℚ, P.degree = 2 ∧ ∀ a ∈ A, ∃ z : ℤ, (a : ℚ) = P.eval (z : ℚ)) := by
  sorry

end Green47

findings.description:
The second disjunct makes EVERY element of A lie in P(ℤ): `∃ P : Polynomial ℚ, P.degree = 2 ∧ ∀ a ∈ A, ∃ z : ℤ, (a : ℚ) = P.eval (z : ℚ)`. Read this literally and the right-hand side of `green_47` is false, for a reason that has nothing to do with the inverse large sieve problem. So the formal statement is settled (answer False) while the problem is open.

Counterexample: A = {q² : q prime, q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ∪ {2}.

(1) The hypothesis holds for every prime p ≥ 3.
- If p ≡ ±1 (mod 8), then 2 is a square mod p, so A mod p lies in the (p+1)/2 squares.
- If p ≡ ±3 (mod 8), then q ≠ p, so each q² is a nonzero square. Hence A mod p lies in {nonzero squares} ∪ {2}, which has (p−1)/2 + 1 = (p+1)/2 classes.
- I proved this in Lean for the exact hypothesis of `green_47`, `∀ᶠ p in atTop, Nat.Prime p → Set.ncard ((fun a : ℕ => (a : ZMod p)) '' A) ≤ (p + 1) / 2`, using only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. A C check over all odd p ≤ 3000 shows the bound is attained.

(2) The first disjunct fails. |A ∩ Iic X| ≥ #{q ≤ √X prime : q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ~ √X/log X, so the ratio to √X/log^100 X tends to infinity. Numerically there are 74,372 elements up to X = 4·10^12. Even without the prime number theorem for progressions this follows: a bound O(√X/log^100 X) would make Σ_{p≡1 (8)} log p/p converge by summing over dyadic blocks. Mathlib's `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt.not_summable_residueClass_prime_div` says it diverges.

(3) The second disjunct fails. Suppose A ⊆ P(ℤ) with P = αx²+βx+γ ∈ ℚ[x]. Take a large prime p ≡ 1 (mod 8).
- A mod p is the full set Sq of squares: 0 comes from q = p; each nonzero square k² comes from a prime q ≡ 1 (mod 8) with q ≡ k (mod p), by Dirichlet; and 2 is a square.
- A mod p lies inside P(F_p) = α·Sq + c′, where c′ = γ − β²/(4α). Both sets have (p+1)/2 elements, so Sq = α·Sq + c′.
- Sum the elements of each side. Σ_{s∈Sq} s = ½ Σ_x x² = 0 for p > 3, so c′(p+1)/2 ≡ 0 (mod p), i.e. c′ ≡ 0 (mod p).
- This holds for infinitely many p, so c′ = 0 and P = α(x − x₀)².
- 49 ∈ P(ℤ) forces α to be a rational square. Then 2 ∈ P(ℤ) would make 2 a rational square, a contradiction.

So `∀ A, hyp → (≪-bound ∨ A ⊆ P(ℤ))` is false. The same A has every element except 2 in the image of x², so it satisfies the quadratic-structure alternative of the Green–Harper conjecture, which allows finitely many exceptions. Separately, `A : Set ℕ` may contain 0, which the literal version would also have to fit into P(ℤ). The fix below absorbs this too.
findings.source_evidence:
Green, 100 Open Problems, Problem 47 (https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf): "Suppose that A ⊂ N is a set with the property that |A (mod p)| ≤ ½(p+1) for all sufficiently large p. ... However, is it true that either |A ∩ [X]| ≪ X^{1/2}/log^{100} X, or A is contained in the image of Z under a quadratic map φ : Q → Q? For background on this question see [154, 172, 303, 304]."

The background paper [GH14], cited by the file (Green–Harper, arXiv:1311.6176), states the conjecture precisely as Conjecture 1.6: "Suppose that A is a set of positive integers and that |A mod p| ≤ ½(p+1) for all sufficiently large primes p. Then one of the following options holds: (i) (Quadratic structure) There is a rational quadratic ψ such that all except finitely many elements of A are contained in ψ(Q); (ii) (Better than large sieve) For each integer k there are arbitrarily large values of X such that |A[X]| < X^{1/2}/log^k X." The same paper's Theorem 1.5 also uses "all except finitely many".

Croot–Mao–Pohoata–Yip (arXiv:2607.15311, 2026) cite Green's Problem 47 and restate the Green–Harper conjecture with "all but finitely many elements of A lie in ψ(Q)".
findings.suggested_fix:
Allow finitely many exceptions in the quadratic alternative, and update the theorem docstring to match:

```lean
      ∨ (∃ P : Polynomial ℚ, P.degree = 2 ∧
          {a ∈ A | ¬ ∃ z : ℤ, (a : ℚ) = P.eval (z : ℚ)}.Finite)
```

That is, all but finitely many elements of A lie in P(ℤ). This is equivalent to Green–Harper's "all except finitely many elements lie in ψ(ℚ)": by GH14 Lemma A.1, ψ(ℚ) ∩ ℤ ⊆ ψ̃(ℤ) for the rational quadratic ψ̃(x) = ψ(x/a). The repaired statement typechecks. Under it, the counterexample satisfies the quadratic alternative with P = X², exceptional set ⊆ {2}; I checked this in Lean.

review.notes:
Lean experiments (in /workspace/review):
- cex.lean proves `Cex.hyp`: the counterexample A satisfies the exact mod-p hypothesis of `green_47`, with no sorry and only the standard axioms.
- fix.lean checks that the repaired statement elaborates, and proves that A satisfies the repaired quadratic alternative with P = X².
- Parts (2) and (3) of the counterexample (growth, and no single quadratic image) are argued on paper. They use only Dirichlet's theorem, whose qualitative form and the divergence of Σ Λ(p)/p over a residue class are in Mathlib, plus elementary finite-field sums. They are not formalised because that would take hundreds of lines.

Other checks, all fine:
- `(p + 1) / 2` is ℕ-division, but it is exact for the odd primes the eventual quantifier covers.
- `A ∩ Set.Iic X` counts 0 as well. This changes the count by at most 1, which is irrelevant because √X/log^100 X → ∞.
- `≪` is `Asymptotics.IsBigO atTop` on ℕ → ℝ (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Analysis/Asymptotics/Basic.lean), matching the source's ≪.
- `P.degree = 2` over ℚ with integer arguments matches "image of ℤ under a quadratic map ℚ → ℚ".
- The `answer(sorry)` polarity is positive, matching "is it true that either … or …".

Green's first alternative (a ≪ bound with the exponent 100, for all large X) differs from Green–Harper's alternative (ii) (for each k, arbitrarily large X with |A[X]| < X^{1/2}/log^k X). The file follows [Gr24] here, which is legitimate, and I found no trivial counterexample to that part.

Status: `research open` is correct. Green's list has no update note for Problem 47, and the 2026 Croot–Mao–Pohoata–Yip paper still treats the inverse large sieve conjecture as open, with partial results only. The defect is in the statement, not the status tag. Stated literally, the claim has an easy negative answer; the intended problem remains open.

not_demonstrated.reason: The RHS is false via A = {q² : q prime, q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ∪ {2}. Only the mod-p hypothesis for A is elementary; it is proved in Lean in about 70 lines but does not by itself show falsity. The other two parts need real number theory. Failure of the ≪ bound needs a quantitative Dirichlet-type count of primes ≡ ±1 (mod 8), derived from the divergence of Σ Λ(p)/p over a residue class via a dyadic summation. Showing no degree-2 P ∈ ℚ[X] covers A needs Dirichlet mod 8p plus finite-field power sums, or Pell theory. Neither is a few-line proof.

submission.summary: No trivial-proof file was produced. The finding against Green47.green_47 is that the literal "A is contained in P(ℤ)" alternative makes the statement false via A = {q² : q prime, q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ∪ {2}. Its refutation combines a formalised mod-p hypothesis check with two steps that need real analytic and algebraic number theory: a prime count in residue classes, and ruling out every rational quadratic. So it cannot be shown in a few lines. The file under review is unchanged.
submission.gave_up_reason: The only reported misformalization, Green47.green_47, is refuted by the counterexample A = {q² : q prime, q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ∪ {2}, but the refutation needs real mathematics. Only the mod-p hypothesis part is elementary; it is formalised in about 70 lines (/workspace/review/cex.lean) and alone does not show the defect. Breaking the ≪ √X/log¹⁰⁰X bound needs a counting lower bound for primes ≡ ±1 (mod 8), which Mathlib only has as divergence of Σ Λ(p)/p over a residue class; turning that into a count takes a dyadic summation argument. Ruling out every degree-2 P ∈ ℚ[X] with A ⊆ P(ℤ) needs Dirichlet's theorem mod 8p, reduction of P mod p and power sums over 𝔽_p (or Pell theory). No junk-value shortcut exists. Any simpler witness that separates the literal "every element in P(ℤ)" from "all but finitely many" needs comparable arguments: sets of at most 3 elements are always coverable, {0,1,2,3} needs Fermat's no-four-squares-in-AP theorem, and squares ∪ {2} needs a mod-p or Pell argument. So nothing admits a short, honest proof, and I did not create /workspace/review/trivial_proof.lean.

submission.summary: In green_47, the quadratic alternative no longer requires every element of A to lie in P(ℤ). It now says all but finitely many do: `∃ P : Polynomial ℚ, P.degree = 2 ∧ {a ∈ A | ¬ ∃ z : ℤ, (a : ℚ) = P.eval (z : ℚ)}.Finite`. This is the "all except finitely many" form of Green–Harper (GH14, Conjecture 1.7); by GH14 Lemma A.1, their ψ(ℚ) form is equivalent to this ℤ-image form. It also makes a 0 in `A : Set ℕ` harmless. The hypothesis, Green's ≪ X^{1/2}/log^100 X alternative, `answer(sorry)`, the `research open` category and the AMS tag are unchanged. The docstring keeps Green's wording and adds a short note: finite exceptions are allowed following GH14 Conjecture 1.7, because read literally the question is trivially false via {q² : q prime, q ≡ ±1 (mod 8)} ∪ {2}. My earlier review cited 'Conjecture 1.6'; the correct number is 1.7 (1.6 is the three-alternative theorem), and the docstring uses 1.7. The file compiles with only the `declaration uses sorry` warning. The prebuilt module file still holds the old statement, so I tested a verbatim copy in a scratch file: it parses as `{a | a ∈ A ∧ ¬∃ z, ↑a = eval ↑z P}.Finite`, the old counterexample satisfies the new alternative with P = X² (only exception 2), and sets of squares satisfy it with no exceptions. Nothing else under /opt/formal-conjectures was touched; the `lakefile.toml` change and the `run/` directory predate this session.
